blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — niacin extended-release flushing management
stem: A client prescribed niacin extended-release tablets reports bothersome flushing after doses. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Ask whether aspirin is appropriate; if approved, take it about 30 minutes before niacin and avoid alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around the time of dosing.
options.B: Take niacin on an empty stomach and increase the dose rapidly because faster dose escalation decreases flushing and improves tolerance compared with gradual titration.
options.C: Use any available NSAID before each dose because all anti-inflammatory drugs are considered interchangeable with aspirin for the labeled flushing-prevention strategy.
options.D: Treat flushing as proof that cardiovascular evaluation is unnecessary because niacin-associated warmth and redness cannot overlap with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.

rationale: Current niacin extended-release labeling states that flushing is common and more likely with therapy initiation or dose increases. The patient information advises asking the doctor whether aspirin can be used; aspirin up to the recommended dose of 325 mg about 30 minutes before niacin can help reduce flushing. The label also advises avoiding hot beverages, alcohol, and spicy foods around dosing and taking extended-release niacin with a low-fat snack rather than on an empty stomach. It separately teaches patients to distinguish flushing from possible myocardial-infarction symptoms. Therefore A is correct. B reverses the administration/titration teaching, C overgeneralizes the labeled aspirin strategy, and D is unsafe.
educational_objective: Teach evidence-based strategies for niacin extended-release flushing: prescriber-approved aspirin shortly before the dose, avoidance of common flushing triggers, appropriate administration and titration, and continued attention to symptoms that could represent a cardiovascular emergency.

source_claim_supported: Niacin ER flushing may be reduced with prescriber-approved aspirin about 30 minutes before dosing and avoidance of alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods; flushing should still be distinguished from possible myocardial-infarction symptoms.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: recognize common adverse effects; provide medication teaching; distinguish expected effects from symptoms requiring further evaluation.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as complete flushing-management statements of comparable length.
Preserved the labeled aspirin timing and trigger-avoidance teaching without suggesting unsupervised prophylaxis.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely matches current niacin ER labeling. The residual length cue was removed before closure; no second defensible teaching statement remains.
